claims.text: High-temperature aging causes segregation in non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys.
High-temperature aging precipitates Mg-rich intermetallic phases in these alloys.
Mg-rich intermetallic phases act as nucleation sites for continuous protective oxide layers.
The aging-induced evolution changes corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior relative to the initial metastable state.
The initial cast alloy has a primarily BCC solid-solution matrix.
Mg and the other elements are homogeneously distributed in the initial state.
The initial state lacks well-defined Mg-rich intermetallic phases.
Annealing at approximately 600–700 °C promotes phase evolution in the proposed Mg-containing alloy.
The resulting Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates form at grain boundaries and within the matrix.
The Mg-rich precipitates oxidize preferentially.
Preferential oxidation of Mg-rich precipitates facilitates growth of an adherent protective oxide scale.
The protective oxide scale reduces further oxygen ingress.
The protective oxide scale retards corrosive attack relative to the homogeneous metastable state.
Aging will measurably increase Mg-rich precipitate density.
Aged samples will form thinner, more uniform, and better-adherent oxide layers than as-cast samples.
Aged samples will have lower corrosion rates than as-cast samples.
Aged samples will have improved high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to as-cast samples.
The as-cast baseline has a mixed-phase microstructure.
The as-cast baseline forms thicker, discontinuous oxide scales and has higher corrosion rates than the aged state.
The proposed effect is limited to an aging window up to about 700 °C and may disappear under substantially different environmental aggressiveness.

contradictions.description: The same as-cast initial state is described as having a homogeneous elemental distribution and a primarily BCC solid-solution matrix, but also as having a mixed-phase microstructure. These descriptions are not necessarily impossible together, but the identity, composition, and distribution of the additional phases are left unresolved, creating an internal inconsistency.
